title: Future Ready Lawyer 2026: Building Confidence in an AI Era
author: Wolters Kluwer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source accepts that AI will restructure rather than wholesale replace legal work and materially develops the cluster’s junior-pipeline thesis. It links reduced junior roles to a future shortage of senior human verifiers, while proposing early AI literacy, preserved analytical training, multidisciplinary talent development, secure tools and performance-based pricing. Its claims are primarily expert predictions and recommendations, not measured employment evidence.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts that AI is reshaping legal-service value capture and materially develops the proposition with survey-based expectations that efficiency will weaken hourly billing and redirect more work to ALSPs. It also qualifies these forecasts by treating them as expectations rather than evidence of completed market-wide change.
qs: 62% of legal department respondents expect AI driven efficiency to reduce the importance of the traditional billable hour, favoring fixed fee and alternative billing models.

More than half of respondents predict that tasks such as legal research, document automation, and contract drafting will increasingly be outsourced to ALSPs, pushing traditional law firms to evolve and focus on high value work.

st.t: AI governance: Literacy and benchmarking build capacity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s capacity-building framing by presenting practical AI literacy and continuous human supervision as prerequisites for productive professional use. Its productivity and pricing claims are explicitly predictive or anecdotal rather than measured, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caveats; it does not materially address benchmarking or courtroom governance.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source directly accepts the cluster’s central proposition: automating junior work risks eroding the future expertise required for human verification. It likewise advocates early AI literacy while preserving analytical and interpretive skill-development pathways; its hybrid-talent and secure-tool recommendations are complementary rather than a material reframing.
qs: Human oversight remains essential: AI outputs must be reviewed through sound legal reasoning and ethical judgment by a human in — or at least on — the loop.
To maintain this balance, organizations should integrate AI literacy into early legal training while preserving pathways for developing core analytical and interpretive skills needed for legal work.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core account that AI gains depend on integrated workflow adoption, training, governance and human verification rather than tool deployment alone. Its respondent-reported efficiency gains, pricing observations and warnings about junior training also align with the synthesis, although it provides limited evidence that corporate legal departments specifically will capture the gains or drive market-wide insourcing.
qs: - Successful adoption of AI requires ongoing investment in training, ethical frameworks, and seamless integration into daily workflows.
Human oversight remains essential: AI outputs must be reviewed through sound legal reasoning and ethical judgment by a human in — or at least on — the loop.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The report accepts that widespread AI use and reported task-level gains are insufficient without dependable organizational integration. It identifies training, process integration, ethics, privacy and change resistance as material barriers, and makes continued investment in governance and workflow integration conditions of successful adoption. Its revenue findings are post-adoption reports rather than causal proof of firm-wide value.
qs: The most frequently mentioned obstacles include ethical and data privacy concerns (39%), lack of adequate training and resources (39%), difficulties integrating AI into existing processes, and resistance to change.
- Successful adoption of AI requires ongoing investment in training, ethical frameworks, and seamless integration into daily workflows.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s preference for AI-assisted legal work with human judgment, training and safeguards rather than autonomous substitution. Its reported efficiency gains reinforce AI’s capacity-expansion potential, while its insistence on human review and secure integration aligns with the cluster’s risk-management model. However, it addresses professional and organisational use, not direct-to-consumer access, remedies or the distribution of verification risk.
qs: 62% of respondents report weekly time savings of 6–20%, averaging nearly 10% of the workweek, enabling a shift from routine tasks to strategic work.
Human oversight remains essential: AI outputs must be reviewed through sound legal reasoning and ethical judgment by a human in — or at least on — the loop.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central concerns that AI may reduce junior roles while weakening the expertise pipeline, and that reliable human verification requires preserved legal reasoning and ethical judgment. It also aligns with the cluster’s recommended adaptation through early AI literacy, continued development of core legal skills, mixed legal-technology talent and secure approved tools. Its claims are mainly conditional recommendations rather than empirical evidence of profession-wide restructuring.
qs: Human oversight remains essential: AI outputs must be reviewed through sound legal reasoning and ethical judgment by a human in — or at least on — the loop.
To maintain this balance, organizations should integrate AI literacy into early legal training while preserving pathways for developing core analytical and interpretive skills needed for legal work.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: AI is already generating measurable gains by automating bounded routine tasks and shifting lawyers toward strategic work, while human verification, training, workflow integration and preservation of junior skill development remain necessary. Its pricing and ALSP claims are presented as predictions rather than settled outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s caution.
qs: 62% of respondents report weekly time savings of 6–20%, averaging nearly 10% of the workweek, enabling a shift from routine tasks to strategic work.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s account of broad AI adoption producing reported efficiency gains while altering provider allocation and pricing expectations. Its survey evidence anticipates more work moving to ALSPs and reduced reliance on hourly billing, while its expert commentary reinforces human oversight, training and preservation of junior-development pathways. These are primarily self-reported outcomes and forecasts, consistent with the cluster’s caution that market-wide transformation remains incomplete.
qs: 62% of legal department respondents expect AI driven efficiency to reduce the importance of the traditional billable hour, favoring fixed fee and alternative billing models.

More than half of respondents predict that tasks such as legal research, document automation, and contract drafting will increasingly be outsourced to ALSPs, pushing traditional law firms to evolve and focus on high value work.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The source supports AI augmentation rather than lawyer replacement and makes continuous human supervision central to responsible use. Its recommendation to build AI literacy through low-stakes familiar uses also aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on competence and training, though these are expert predictions and recommendations rather than empirical evidence or a developed regulatory framework.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective, governed augmentation rather than prohibition: it recommends task-embedded training focused on reviewing outputs and spotting risks, while treating ethics and data protection as conditions of adoption. Its survey indicates widespread use but does not test productivity gains, verification costs or staffing effects.
qs: -  Training works best when it focuses on prompt strategy, outcome review, and risk spotting within real tasks.
Bans and restrictions do not work — lawyers will find a way to use AI anyway, but they will do so in an uncontrolled and potentially dangerous manner.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s central proposition that AI will automate routine production and shift lawyers toward strategic, judgment-intensive work rather than replace them. It also supports bounded automation through human verification, warns that reduced junior work may damage the expert-development pipeline, and treats pricing effects as variable rather than uniform.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts that AI can take over simpler legal tasks and reduce junior roles while preserving essential human oversight, legal judgment and expertise. It also supports the cluster’s adaptation themes through recommendations for early AI literacy, hybrid legal-technology talent and secure approved tools. Its claims are primarily predictions and recommendations, not evidence of aggregate employment or savings outcomes.

st.an: The report aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: AI reallocates routine legal tasks toward higher-value work but requires human verification, training, workflow integration and broader organisational readiness. Its adoption, efficiency and revenue claims are self-reported, while its pricing and labour effects are predictions, so it supports rather than materially extends the synthesis’s more cautious evidence assessment.

kp.k: Survey covers 810 lawyers, surveyed in August 2025
kp.d: The 2026 report draws on an online survey of 810 lawyers in law firms and corporate legal departments, conducted August 8–25, 2025. The document describes coverage as the U.S., China and eight European countries, but its country list names nine European countries. Its findings concern respondents' reported practices, benefits and expectations; the report also includes separately attributed expert commentary.
qs: The study was conducted using an online survey administered to a group of 810 lawyers from law firms and corporate legal departments in the U.S., China, and eight European countries.
The survey was conducted online for Wolters Kluwer by a leading international research organization from August 8 to August 25, 2025.
Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Belgium, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, and Hungary

kp.k: AI use is widespread across routine legal tasks
kp.d: The report states that 92% of legal professionals use at least one AI tool and that over 90% of respondents use one in their daily workflow. It identifies research and analysis, argument development, contract drafting and document review as leading applications, describing adoption across law firms, corporate legal departments and business consulting practices.
qs: 92% of legal professionals now use at least one AI tool
Over 90% of respondents report using at least one AI tool in their daily workflow
AI is most used for legal research and analysis, developing legal arguments, drafting contracts, and reviewing documents.

kp.k: Respondents report time savings and opportunities for strategic work
kp.d: The report says 62% of respondents save 6–20% of weekly working time through AI, averaging nearly 10% of the workweek. It argues that automating routine tasks enables more strategic, high-value work, while identifying ongoing training, ethical frameworks and workflow integration as conditions of successful adoption.
qs: 62% of respondents report weekly time savings of 6–20%, averaging nearly 10% of the workweek, enabling a shift from routine tasks to strategic work.
Successful adoption of AI requires ongoing investment in training, ethical frameworks, and seamless integration into daily workflows.

kp.k: Revenue increases are reported following AI adoption
kp.d: The report presents revenue growth as a reported benefit of AI adoption: 52% of respondents report increases after adoption, while approximately 50% report increases of 6%–20%. These are reported outcomes, alongside the report's broader argument that holistic AI adoption supports quality and client trust.
qs: 52% of respondents reported revenue increases after adopting AI
Approximately 50% of respondents reported that revenue has increased by 6%–20%
Legal organizations that embrace AI holistically are better positioned to deliver consistent, high-quality outcomes and build lasting client trust.

kp.k: Legal departments anticipate declining reliance on hourly billing
kp.d: Among legal department respondents, 62% expect AI efficiency to reduce the importance of the billable hour in favour of fixed-fee and alternative arrangements. This is an expectation about business-model change, not a measured decline in hourly billing. The report also argues that improved work and budget estimation supports flat-fee and value-based arrangements.
qs: 62% of legal department respondents expect AI driven efficiency to reduce the importance of the traditional billable hour, favoring fixed fee and alternative billing models.
AI also enables better work and budget estimation, increasing trust in flat fee and value based arrangements.

kp.k: Some clients may pay premiums for faster outcomes
kp.d: ILTA CEO Joy Heath Rush reports hearing general counsel express differing preferences: some want lower outside-counsel bills, whereas others would pay the same or more for speed and better results. She predicts performance premiums may become more common where AI delivers answers sooner and gives clients more time to act; this is conference-based commentary rather than a survey finding.
qs: Some certainly want their bills lowered. However, others are happy to pay the same — or more — for faster results and better outcomes.

Although it is not unusual for clients to pay “performance premiums” for certain work, that may become more common if AI can help clients obtain answers more quickly, giving them greater time to plan, pivot, etc.

kp.k: Respondents predict increased outsourcing to ALSPs
kp.d: More than half of respondents expect legal research, document automation and contract drafting to be increasingly outsourced to alternative legal service providers. The report frames this anticipated change as pressure on traditional law firms to focus on high-value work and develop collaboration and service-diversification models.
qs: More than half of respondents predict that tasks such as legal research, document automation, and contract drafting will increasingly be outsourced to ALSPs, pushing traditional law firms to evolve and focus on high value work.
This encourages new collaboration models and service diversification.

kp.k: Ethics, privacy, training and resistance constrain further adoption
kp.d: Respondents identify ethical and data privacy concerns (39%), inadequate training (39%) and resistance to change (35%) as leading implementation barriers. The FAQ also identifies difficulties integrating AI into existing processes. These findings qualify the report's account of already widespread use.
qs: The top challenges to further AI implementation are ethical concerns related to AI and data privacy (39%), inadequate training (39%), and resistance to change (35%).

The most frequently mentioned obstacles include ethical and data privacy concerns (39%), lack of adequate training and resources (39%), difficulties integrating AI into existing processes, and resistance to change.

kp.k: Security concerns exceed reported organizational preparedness
kp.d: The report says 35% cite cybersecurity as a significant concern. Its FAQ reports 46% identifying data-protection compliance and safeguarding sensitive information against cyberattacks as key challenges, and 43% identifying client confidentiality. Only about one third of organizations feel very prepared to manage these risks amid remote work, cloud technology and AI.
qs: 35% of respondents cite cybersecurity as a significant concern, however few organizations feel very prepared to address those challenges

46% of respondents point to compliance with data protection regulations and safeguarding sensitive information against cyberattacks as key challenges, while 43% highlight ensuring client confidentiality.
Only about one third of organizations feel “very prepared” to manage these risks, despite the increasing importance of remote work, cloud technologies, and AI.

kp.k: Security responses combine technical controls and outside expertise
kp.d: Reported security practices include multi-factor authentication (55%), encrypted communications (50%), regular audits (49%) and external IT and cybersecurity expertise (55%). The report also recommends staff training and restrictions on unauthorized cloud tools. Privacy1 founder Marie José Bonthuis separately argues that ethics and data protection should be incorporated early in design to build trust, with transparency about data users and uses.
qs: The most common practices include multi factor authentication (55%), encrypted communication tools (50%), regular security audits (49%), and cooperation with external IT and cybersecurity experts (55%).
Regular staff training and restricting access to unauthorized cloud tools are also essential.
By incorporating these aspects early in the design, trust increases. This includes being transparent about which parties (inside or outside the EU) use the data and in what way.

kp.k: Secure approved tools are recommended against shadow AI
kp.d: Tomasz Zalewski argues that failing to supply suitable secure AI tools drives lawyers toward uncontrolled shadow AI, creating ethical and reputational risks. His recommendation is proactive provision of approved tools rather than bans; this is expert advice, not a measured finding about the effectiveness of restrictions.
qs: If they do not get secure tools, they will have “shadow AI” and situations that are dangerous in terms of ethics and reputation.
The only effective solution is a proactive approach: providing lawyers with secure, approved AI tools that meet their needs.
Bans and restrictions do not work — lawyers will find a way to use AI anyway, but they will do so in an uncontrolled and potentially dangerous manner.

kp.k: Demand grows for specialized regulatory and cross-border expertise
kp.d: The report says 44% of participants report increased demand for sanctions, export controls, international arbitration and cross-border transaction expertise. It relates this demand to global business complexity and geopolitical risks, also citing cybersecurity concerns (35%) and regulatory scrutiny and compliance requirements (33%). Its assertion that AI will be critical to managing demand is forward-looking.
qs: 44% of survey participants report increased demand for expertise in sanctions, export controls, international arbitration, and cross-border transactions.
Cybersecurity concerns (35%) and regulatory scrutiny and compliance requirements (33%) continue to intensify.
Effective use of AI will be critical for managing these expanding demands.

kp.k: Technology competence increasingly shapes recruitment and development
kp.d: The report states that 70% of lawyers regard technological skills as important or very important and that 75% of legal departments place even stronger emphasis on them. WEI Xin advocates recruiting and developing people who combine legal experience with technical expertise, including internally supported legal-technology clubs or study groups led by enthusiastic young professionals.
qs: Technological skills are becoming essential—70% of lawyers consider them important or very important, and 75% of legal departments place even stronger emphasis on them.
The most valuable talent today are those who possess both legal experience and technological expertise, and we need targeted reforms in both recruitment and talent development.

Organizations may establish legal‑technology clubs or study groups internally, appointing the most passionate young professionals as leaders, and providing them with institutional support such as funding, training opportunities, and access to external technical experts for guidance.

kp.k: Junior displacement could undermine future human verification capacity
kp.d: Frauke Rostalski frames AI's takeover of simpler tasks as reducing junior roles and warns that replacing all junior lawyers could erode the future senior-expert pool needed to check AI outputs. She recommends early AI literacy alongside preserved pathways for analytical and interpretive skill formation, emphasizing human legal reasoning and ethical judgment when reviewing outputs. This is an expert warning, not quantified evidence of job losses.
qs: As AI takes over simpler legal tasks, reducing junior roles, firms must ensure traditional legal skills are not lost.
Human oversight remains essential: AI outputs must be reviewed through sound legal reasoning and ethical judgment by a human in — or at least on — the loop.

Replacing all junior lawyers with AI risks eroding the future pool of (senior-) experts needed for humanin/ on-the-loop oversight and could potentially undermine both professional standards and trust in AI-assisted legal work.

kp.k: Strategic-work transformation is conditional on continuous human supervision
kp.d: Licia Garotti predicts substantial change in legal service delivery and value measurement over the next five years. Rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, she envisages productivity tools enabling an '80/20 reversal' toward analysis and strategic advice, expressly conditional on human supervision without exception.
qs: Over the next five years, AI is likely to significantly transform the provision of legal services and the measurement of value.

Instead of replacing lawyers, AI tools that demonstrate a significant increase in productivity (think document review) allow lawyers to move from routine work to high-value strategic advice: the '80/20 reversal,' where lawyers spend 80% of their time analyzing rather than gathering information; provided that, with no exception, human supervision is always in place.

kp.k: AI literacy training should connect familiarity with practical judgment
kp.d: Dyane O’Leary recommends beginning AI literacy through low-stakes use on familiar personal topics. Greg Lambert separately recommends task-based training in prompting, output review and risk identification, with ethical guidance embedded in realistic work examples. These are practitioner and educator recommendations rather than tested training-effectiveness findings.
qs: What I mean by that is someone won’t grasp it professionally until they start to familiarize themselves with it in a low-stakes, casual environment with topics familiar to them — cooking, travel, home repair, whatever the case may be.
Training works best when it focuses on prompt strategy, outcome review, and risk spotting within real tasks.
Ethical guidance lands when it is embedded in examples that match the rhythm of daily work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wolters Kluwer presents AI as a mainstream legal-work tool associated with time savings and revenue growth, and reports expectations of alternative billing, increased ALSP outsourcing, and changing skills requirements. Expert commentators add predictions about task substitution, junior staffing, supervision, and client value.
pts.d: The report states that 92% of legal professionals use at least one AI tool, particularly for research and analysis, developing arguments, drafting contracts, and document review. It reports that 62% save 6–20% of their weekly time, with the FAQ describing average savings as nearly 10% of the workweek, and argues that automation frees lawyers for strategic work. It reports that 52% experienced revenue increases after AI adoption; a separate bullet says approximately 50% reported increases of 6–20%. On business models, 62% of legal department respondents expect AI efficiencies to reduce the importance of hourly billing. The report also claims AI improves work and budget estimation, supporting fixed-fee and value-based arrangements. More than half of respondents predict increased outsourcing of research, document automation, and contract drafting to alternative legal service providers, pushing traditional firms toward higher-value work, collaboration, and service diversification. Technological skills are described as increasingly essential: 70% of lawyers consider them important or very important, and the FAQ reports stronger emphasis among 75% of legal departments. The report says effective AI use will be critical to handling expanding specialist compliance demands; it attributes those demands to global business complexity and geopolitical risks, rather than to AI itself. Licia Garotti predicts substantial transformation in service provision and value measurement, with augmentation rather than replacement and an '80/20 reversal' toward analysis. Joy Heath Rush suggests AI-enabled speed and better outcomes may make performance premiums more common, while some clients seek lower bills. Frauke Rostalski states that AI taking over simpler tasks reduces junior roles and warns that eliminating juniors could erode the future senior-expert pool. WEI Xin identifies combined legal and technological expertise as especially valuable. Tomasz Zalewski predicts uncontrolled 'shadow AI' if firms do not provide approved tools and argues bans will not prevent use. Dyane O’Leary advocates low-stakes personal experimentation as a precursor to professional AI literacy; Greg Lambert argues that task-based training improves learning; Marie José Bonthuis argues that incorporating ethics and data protection early increases trust.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The numerical findings are based on a commissioned online survey of 810 legal professionals; market forecasts are respondents’ expectations, while the additional claims rest on expert commentary and, in one instance, a conference anecdote.
pts.d: Wolters Kluwer describes quantitative interviews conducted online by an unnamed leading international research organization on August 8–25, 2025, involving 810 lawyers in law firms and corporate legal departments. Usage, time savings, revenue changes, skills priorities, and barriers are respondent reports. Billing and ALSP figures measure expectations, not observed future market changes. The supplied landing-page text gives no task benchmarks, independently measured productivity or revenue outcomes, or causal comparison establishing that AI produced the reported revenue growth. It also does not supply sampling, weighting, response-rate, or subgroup-size details. Its geographical description says eight European countries but lists nine: Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Belgium, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, and Hungary, alongside the U.S. and China. The general claims about AI enabling better estimation, higher-quality outcomes, and trust have no separate empirical demonstration in this text. Garotti, Rostalski, O’Leary, WEI Xin, Zalewski, Lambert, and Bonthuis provide professional opinions or recommendations rather than cited studies. Rush specifically bases her account of differing client preferences on a recent conference panel of general counsel; the prediction that performance premiums could become more common is Rush’s own inference. The publisher identifies itself as a provider of legal and compliance solutions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported adoption and benefits reflect August 2025 survey responses published as the 2026 report; most forecasts have no fixed deadline, except Garotti’s five-year horizon. Benefits are repeatedly conditioned on supervision, training, workflow integration, security, and ethics.
pts.d: The report presents adoption as current and time savings as weekly, based on the August 2025 fieldwork. Revenue increases are described as occurring after implementation, without a defined measurement period or adoption duration. Billing changes, ALSP outsourcing, and evolving skill needs are directional predictions without specified dates. Garotti explicitly predicts change over the next five years and makes the shift to strategic work conditional on productivity-enhancing tools and human supervision without exception. Rush’s performance-premium prediction is conditional on AI producing faster answers and better outcomes; she does not predict universal fee reductions or increases. Rostalski’s warning about the future expert pipeline concerns the risk of replacing all juniors, not a dated or quantified forecast of employment losses, and she insists on human review using legal reasoning and ethical judgment. Wolters Kluwer conditions successful adoption on ongoing training, ethical frameworks, and workflow integration. Survey respondents identify ethics and privacy concerns (39%), inadequate training (39%), and resistance to change (35%) as barriers. Cybersecurity is a significant concern for 35%; the FAQ says only about one third feel very prepared to manage the information-security and compliance risks it discusses. Zalewski conditions safer use on providing secure, approved tools rather than relying on bans. Bonthuis treats ethics, data protection, and transparency about data use as prerequisites for success, rather than merely obstacles.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes affect law-firm providers, corporate legal-department buyers, ALSPs, clients, and lawyers at different career stages; the document does not specify firm-size impacts or access-to-justice outcomes.
pts.d: For law firms and individual lawyers, the report describes less time on routine research, review, and drafting, more scope for strategic advice, potential revenue gains, and pressure to change pricing and develop technological skills. Corporate legal departments are both AI users and buyers expecting less reliance on hourly billing, greater cost transparency, and improved budget estimation. Rush describes heterogeneous buyer preferences: some general counsel want lower outside-counsel bills, while others would pay the same or more for speed and outcomes. ALSPs are predicted to receive more outsourced legal work, distinct from software sales by legal-tech vendors; traditional firms are expected to respond through specialization and collaboration. Junior lawyers face potential reductions in simpler work and roles, while Rostalski warns that future senior lawyers and organizations needing human verification could suffer from weakened training pathways. WEI Xin’s recommendations focus on recruiting and developing people who combine legal experience with technological capability, including young professionals leading internal learning groups. Firm and legal-department leadership face responsibilities for approved tools, staff training, ethical governance, confidentiality, and cybersecurity; clients face corresponding implications for trust and protection of sensitive information. The report also mentions use in business consulting practices, although its stated survey population is lawyers in firms and corporate departments. Specialized practitioners in sanctions, export controls, international arbitration, and cross-border transactions face growing demand that the report says AI will help manage. No quantified distinction is offered between large and small firms, and there is no concrete claim about unmet civil legal need or public access to justice.
